questions.question: According to the introduction, what is the positioning of the PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No.1?

options.A: A guide that shares PDA's views and promotes dialogue between industry and regulators; it is not an industry standard or regulatory guidance
options.B: A mandatory industry standard that replaces the sterile filling chapter of EU GMP Annex 1 and must be followed by every site
options.C: Regulatory guidance already recognized by FDA that can be used directly as the basis for GMP inspections
options.D: A specification standard used only by equipment suppliers when designing machines

questions.explanation: The introduction states that the guide conveys PDA's thinking and encourages dialogue among industry, health authorities and suppliers, and does not itself represent an industry standard or regulatory guidance. It does not replace Annex 1 and is not an FDA guidance; its audience is the whole sterile manufacturing industry, not only equipment makers.

questions.question: According to the scope statement, at what point do regulators and industry consider container-closure integrity (CCI) to be assured?

options.A: When filling is complete, the liquid level is above the minimum mark and 100% IPC has passed
options.B: After the stopper is seated and the raised stopper check has been passed
options.C: After the container is fully closed (including the crimp seal where one is required)
options.D: After the product has completed visual inspection and been labeled

questions.explanation: The Scope states that CCI is assured only once the container is fully closed, and for containers using a crimp seal this includes application of the mechanical seal. A seated stopper alone is not enough; fill level and labeling have nothing to do with whether CCI is established.

questions.question: According to the glossary, in what situation is the "Grade A Air Supply" mainly used?

options.A: Directly above the filling needles inside an open RABS
options.B: To protect vials that are fully stoppered but not yet crimped
options.C: During the aeration phase after isolator biodecontamination
options.D: For semi-stoppered product during loading of a lyophilizer

questions.explanation: Grade A Air Supply is air passed through qualified filters that can achieve Grade A total particle quality, but it does not require continuous total particle monitoring or Grade A viable limits, and the area itself is not classified; it is used specifically to protect vials that are fully stoppered but not yet crimped. The area above the filling needles and semi-stoppered product are true Grade A critical zones, so it does not apply there.

questions.question: According to the glossary, which of the following is a corrective intervention rather than an inherent intervention?

options.A: Aseptic assembly of the filling path
options.B: Container replenishment
options.C: Environmental monitoring sampling during the process
options.D: Clearing a jammed component

questions.explanation: A corrective intervention is carried out to correct or adjust the process and does not necessarily occur on a regular basis, for example clearing a component jam, stopping a leak, adjusting a sensor or replacing a part. Aseptic assembly, container replenishment and environmental sampling are required by procedure and are inherent interventions.

questions.question: According to the scope statement, which technology is explicitly outside the scope of this guide?

options.A: Blow-fill-seal / form-fill-seal
options.B: Prefilled syringes supplied in RTU tubs/nests and filled in an isolator
options.C: Conventional aseptic vial filling using RABS
options.D: Aseptic filling of highly potent products

questions.explanation: The Scope states that blow-fill-seal and form-fill-seal, where the container is formed in line, are not discussed, and refers readers to PDA TR77. RTU syringes and RABS vial filling are subjects of the document; highly potent products are not covered by a complete guide, but are still discussed where appropriate.

questions.question: According to section 1.1.1, which filling environment should be used for highly potent or toxic products (with an OEB/OEL assigned)?

options.A: An oRABS combined with a higher air change rate
options.B: A cRABS or an isolator with a containment design
options.C: Open filling in a conventional cleanroom with a Grade B background
options.D: Any barrier will do, as long as operators wear double sterile gloves and shorten the operation time

questions.explanation: Hazardous products should use a closed RABS or an isolator with containment capability (airflow, pressure cascade), so that the environment, personnel and product are protected at the same time and residues, soiled parts and spills can be handled. An oRABS and an open cleanroom have no containment capability, and gloves cannot replace engineered containment.

questions.question: According to section 1.1.2.2, when inert gas is used to displace the container headspace for oxygen-sensitive products, which point in time is the most important and most effective?

options.A: Pre-gassing the container before filling
options.B: Gassing simultaneously during filling with a double-needle arrangement
options.C: Gassing in the tunnel after filling and before stoppering
options.D: Gassing at the time of closure (stoppering)

questions.explanation: The document lists pre-gassing, gassing during filling, after filling and at closure, and notes that gassing at closure is the most important and most effective method. Incoming liquid displaces gas that was introduced earlier, so the earlier points in time are less effective.

questions.question: According to section 1.1.2.3, which wavelength range of high-energy light most often causes photodegradation?

options.A: About 300 to 500 nm
options.B: 600 to 700 nm (red light)
options.C: 700 to 900 nm (near infrared)
options.D: 1,000 nm and above (infrared)

questions.explanation: The document notes that blue and ultraviolet light carry more energy than red light, and that high-energy wavelengths of 300 to 500 nm most often cause photodegradation, so a characterization study of the photodegradation pathway is recommended first. Red light above 600 nm and infrared light have lower energy. The document also warns that amber vials can make visual inspection more difficult.

questions.question: According to section 1.1.2.5, when handling silicone-free or coated stoppers for syringes, which stoppering method may the filling line need to be designed for?

options.A: Vent-tube mechanical stoppering, because stopper position is most precise when referenced to the finger flange
options.B: Direct pressing in from a vibratory bowl, because line speed is fastest
options.C: Vacuum stoppering, because the stopper may not tolerate the frictional compression of a vent tube
options.D: Manual stoppering, because each stopper position can be visually confirmed

questions.explanation: Silicone-free or coated stoppers may not withstand the mechanical friction and compression of vent-tube stoppering, so vacuum stoppering is often needed; for high-viscosity products vacuum filling may also be needed, to remove air bubbles in the luer channel and reduce splashing. Vent-tube stoppering is exactly the method to be avoided, and manual stoppering adds intervention risk.

questions.question: According to section 1.5, if campaign production is used, what should the APS design cover?

options.A: Only the setup and filling of the first batch of the campaign
options.B: The maximum time between biodecontamination cycles plus the maximum number of interventions representative of a routine campaign
options.C: PUPSIT for every batch is enough, and no separate APS needs to be designed
options.D: A single piggy-back APS after the campaign ends, with no need to cover the setup phase

questions.explanation: A campaign APS must challenge the risk conditions specific to the campaign, such as the longest time between two biodecontamination cycles, together with the maximum number of interventions representative of a routine campaign and the longest use time of the flow path between CIP/SIP cycles. A piggy-back APS can be used, but only if the setup phase is also covered in the APS strategy; PUPSIT cannot replace an APS either.

questions.question: According to section 2.1, below what viscosity is a peristaltic pump (PP) usually suitable?

options.A: About 300,000 mPa-s
options.B: About 100 mPa-s
options.C: About 60 mPa-s
options.D: About 10 mPa-s

questions.explanation: When the product is not viscous (usually below 60 mPa-s), a PP is well suited, and the cleaning and sterilization burden is also smaller than for an RPP. 300,000 mPa-s is the upper limit for an RPP, and about 100 mPa-s is the range for TP and DP.

questions.question: According to section 2.1.2, why does the dose of a PP drift after long operation, and how is this recommended to be controlled?

options.A: The tubing wears and softens, causing drift; correct based on weighing results, with IPC recommended
options.B: Aging roller bearings reduce the speed; replace the servo motor periodically
options.C: Product warming lowers the viscosity; a cooling jacket must be added to the intermediate vessel
options.D: The tubing hardens and the dose rises; calibration once at the start of the batch is enough

questions.explanation: Pump tubing softens through wear, so the delivered dose drifts over time, and a statistical correction based on in-line weighing results is needed; statistical or 100% IPC is therefore strongly recommended. The pump head itself shows little wear over many years, and a single calibration at the start of the batch cannot catch drift that develops gradually.

questions.question: According to section 2.1.2, when PP tubing is divided into three sections for material selection, how should the section downstream of the pump be chosen?

options.A: The same as the section inside the rollers, with high softness to aid recovery
options.B: As soft as possible, to absorb the pulsating pressure from the pump
options.C: This section is the least important and any material may be used
options.D: Lower softness, to avoid deformation under liquid pressure that would affect the dose or cause dripping

questions.explanation: The downstream section does not need to work with the rollers, so a less soft material should be chosen so that it is not distorted by the pressure of the liquid being delivered; deformation in this section would change the dose or cause dripping. Only the section inside the rollers needs to be soft, and the section the document calls the least critical is the one upstream of the pump, not the downstream one.

questions.question: According to section 2.1.3, what problem is common in a PP system if the intermediate vessel is located lower than the filling needles?

options.A: The product drips continuously through siphon action
options.B: Bubbles or air gaps form in the tubing
options.C: The gap between the rollers and the backing plate widens, so the tubing is not squeezed tightly
options.D: The pressure drop across the filter is too high

questions.explanation: If the pump must draw product upward from a vessel located lower than the filling needles, bubbles often form in the tubing. The design should therefore evaluate the relative height of the intermediate vessel and the needles, as well as tube diameter and length; this matters even more when the PP is installed outside the barrier and far from the needles.

questions.question: According to section 2.1.8, the geometry of PP tubing may differ between lots. If 100% IPC is not used, in which period is a higher weighing frequency especially needed?

options.A: Mid-batch, because the tubing temperature is highest then
options.B: Near the end of the batch, because the liquid level in the intermediate vessel is lowest
options.C: At the start of the batch, and also in the wear-in period after long operation
options.D: After every shift change, because of operator handover

questions.explanation: Different tubing lots may have different inner and outer diameters, wall thickness and elasticity, so during setup the fill volume must be adjusted to the tubing lot actually in use. The best practice is 100% IPC; if another strategy is used, a high monitoring frequency must be kept at the start of the batch, and long production runs, when wear begins to affect performance, are also a critical period, to be supported by a risk assessment.

questions.question: According to section 2.2.5, why must an RPP always remain inside the isolator or RABS?

options.A: The servo motor needs Grade A air for cooling
options.B: The pump head is heavy and can only be fixed to the machine deck
options.C: An RPP cannot be CIP/SIP processed and can only be assembled inside
options.D: Product at the point where the piston enters the cylinder is exposed over a small area

questions.explanation: An RPP is an unsealed design lubricated by the product, and where the piston is inserted into the cylinder the product is exposed to the filling environment over a small area, so it must always remain within containment to maintain sterility; a TP or PP can have some components mounted outside. In fact an RPP can be CIP/SIP processed, so the option stating that it cannot be is wrong, and cooling and weight are not reasons the document gives.

questions.question: According to sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.6, if the RPP dose shows no drift between the start and end of a batch, how should the IPC strategy be set?

options.A: The dose is stable, so no IPC is needed and the batch can be released directly
options.B: Statistical IPC can be used, but periodic IPC is still needed to detect underfills caused by air bubbles
options.C: 100% IPC must be used, because the piston and cylinder wear progressively with each stroke and cause drift
options.D: A single IPC check at the start of the batch is enough

questions.explanation: Unlike a PP, an RPP does not drift, so statistical IPC is technically appropriate; periodic IPC is still recommended to catch underfills caused by air bubbles in the line, with the frequency justified by product characteristics and actual data. Doing no IPC or only one check cannot catch bubble problems that arise during the process.

questions.question: According to section 2.2.2, why are the piston and cylinder of an RPP often engraved with serial numbers by the OEM and assembled as matched pairs?

options.A: Tolerances are very tight, and mixing them can cause seizing or problems with dose, dripping or leakage
options.B: To make it easy to track the cumulative sterilization cycles of each pump to calculate the remaining service life
options.C: Regulations require each pump to carry an individual UDI marking
options.D: Different serial numbers represent different fill volume specifications

questions.explanation: The mechanical tolerances between piston and cylinder are very tight, and the serial numbers ensure that matched parts are assembled together, avoiding jamming and seizing, or a loose tolerance that changes the dose or causes needle dripping or leakage. Some materials such as ceramic are exceptions and can be interchanged. The serial numbers are unrelated to UDI, sterilization counts or volume specifications.

questions.question: According to section 2.2.3, how should the intermediate vessel of an RPP be set up when filling low-viscosity products?

options.A: Pressurized, to increase filling speed and reduce bubbles
options.B: As low as possible, to reduce the head pressure
options.C: Vented and kept at a constant level, to keep the head pressure stable
options.D: Under vacuum, to remove dissolved oxygen

questions.explanation: To avoid excessive pressure pushing product out between the piston and cylinder, the intermediate vessel must be vented and kept at a constant level so that the head pressure is stable, which is especially important for low-viscosity products. Pressurized, non-vented intermediate vessels are more often used for high-viscosity products.

questions.question: According to sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.5, what countermeasure can be considered for an RPP if the product is abrasive or prone to crystallization?

options.A: Switch to an SU single-use RPP, replaced every batch
options.B: Add a compatible lubricating oil between the piston and cylinder to reduce friction
options.C: Increase the pump speed so that crystals have no time to deposit
options.D: Switch to a ceramic pump, or relax the tolerance when there is no dripping concern

questions.explanation: Tight tolerances cannot withstand crystals formed during operation, and abrasive products also damage the pump, so the document suggests a ceramic pump or, where there is no dripping concern, a larger tolerance. An RPP can only be lubricated by the product, so adding another lubricant is not appropriate; SU RPPs are available from vendors but rarely used because of price, and are not a countermeasure aimed at this problem.

questions.question: According to section 2.3, why does a time-pressure (TP) system need a separate high-speed PLC?

options.A: To calculate the required valve opening time from real-time pressure and temperature
options.B: To control the speed and acceleration/deceleration of the peristaltic pump rollers
options.C: To record the audit trail to meet Part 11 requirements
options.D: To detect tubing rupture at the pinch valve

questions.explanation: The independent controller of a TP calculates the fill time actually needed from the current pressure and temperature; if a fixed time were relied on, fill accuracy would shift whenever pressure or temperature changed, and low-pressure systems are affected even more by temperature. Rollers are a PP component, and audit trails and rupture detection are not the purpose of this PLC.

questions.question: According to section 2.3.9, what is the limitation of the leak test performed before CIP/SIP of a TP system?

options.A: It deforms the orifice, which then has to be replaced afterwards
options.B: It can only detect failures of the pinch valve motor and the temperature sensor
options.C: It cannot confirm that the orifice is not blocked, so the CIP/SIP process needs to be monitored
options.D: It leaves test gas residue, so extra drying is needed

questions.explanation: During CIP/SIP there is a small risk of the orifice becoming blocked (especially after silicone tubing is replaced, which may leave shavings), and a leak test beforehand cannot confirm that the orifice is not blocked, so the CIP/SIP process should be monitored; the conductivity and temperature sensors are located at the outlet after the needles merge. The document does not mention the other options.

questions.question: According to section 2.3.4, when handling highly potent products, why is it recommended to place the pinch valves of a TP inside the isolator?

options.A: Pinch valves need Grade A air to operate properly
options.B: The tubing is stressed at the pinch valve, so the chance of tubing rupture and leakage is higher
options.C: Placing them outside would invalidate the PLC's temperature compensation
options.D: Regulations explicitly prohibit placing pinch valves outside the barrier

questions.explanation: The pinch valve applies stress to the flexible tubing, so a TP has a higher risk of tubing rupture than other systems (although the tubing is still stressed less than in a PP); for highly potent products the pinch valves should therefore be inside the isolator for containment, where leak detection can be installed and the affected station shut off when a leak is found. No such regulatory prohibition exists, and temperature compensation is unrelated to location.

questions.question: According to section 2.4.4, what is the best practice for detecting a small breach in the diaphragm or tubing of a rolling diaphragm pump (DP)?

options.A: After each batch, remove the diaphragm and tubing and inspect for damage visually with a magnifier
options.B: Rely on 100% IPC to catch containers with abnormal weight and trace them back to the station
options.C: Install a level sensor in the intermediate vessel
options.D: Install a moisture sensor in the vacuum line

questions.explanation: A DP operates under negative pressure, which reduces the ingress of microorganisms and particles, but it can still fail; the best practice is to install a moisture sensor in the vacuum line so that any breach can be dealt with immediately. The diaphragm is a wear part, so its use count should be tracked and it should be replaced before it fails; for highly potent products, placing the mechanical components within containment must also be considered.

questions.question: According to sections 2.4.7 and 2.4.10, how does the installation of a CIP/SIP-type rolling DP differ from a standard one?

options.A: It is installed horizontally, to facilitate drainage after CIP/SIP
options.B: It is installed inverted, to facilitate steam penetration
options.C: It must be installed outside the barrier, to ease connection of the CIP/SIP supply and return lines
options.D: It has no vacuum supply connected, to avoid condensate backflow

questions.explanation: A standard DP is installed vertically, while a CIP/SIP type needs horizontal installation to ensure correct drainage after CIP/SIP; because the orientation changes, the airflow of the cleanroom or isolator must be considered in the design. A DP must always have vacuum to maintain the diaphragm position, so the option of not connecting vacuum is wrong, and the document does not require inverted installation or installation outside the barrier.

questions.question: According to section 4.1.2, what role does the APS play with respect to the duration of a continuous or campaign process?

options.A: The APS is the main means of establishing and validating the process duration
options.B: The duration is established and confirmed separately; the APS incorporates its conditions but is not the main means of validation
options.C: As long as the APS passes, the campaign length can be extended without limit
options.D: The duration follows the isolator supplier's recommendation and needs no validation

questions.explanation: Production duration should be designed according to capacity needs and then confirmed against equipment and process capability; once determined, the duration and the associated interventions and changeover conditions are incorporated into the APS design. However, the APS should not be used as the main means of establishing or validating the process duration (citing Annex 1). When designed and validated properly, a campaign in an isolator can continue for weeks, but it is not unlimited.

questions.question: According to the note in section 4.1.2, what does Annex 1 expect regarding the use time of a liquid sterilizing filter?

options.A: It can be used up to the end of the whole campaign
options.B: At most 72 hours, whether or not validated
options.C: There is no time limit as long as PUPSIT passes
options.D: No longer than one working day, unless validated

questions.explanation: The note cites Annex 1 section 8.95: a liquid sterilizing filter should not be used for longer than one working day unless the process has been validated. For a long campaign it should therefore be considered in advance whether the filter needs to be changed midway, or whether parallel filtration paths should be set up from the start. PUPSIT is an integrity test and is a separate matter from the use time limit.

questions.question: According to section 4.1.4, if a campaign must use an RPP to fill 2 mL and then 14 mL within the same barrier, what is the main problem?

options.A: 14 mL exceeds the upper viscosity limit the RPP can handle
options.B: The fill curves for the two volumes cannot be run in the same recipe
options.C: The pump usually has to be changed; if the barrier must be opened to change it, the campaign is not feasible
options.D: Nested containers must be used to switch the fill volume

questions.explanation: With such a large volume difference the RPP usually has to be replaced; if the barrier must be opened to fit a larger pump, sterility is broken and the campaign is not feasible, so another filling technology may have to be chosen. Viscosity and nested containers have nothing to do with this issue. The document also reminds that the limit for a PP is the number of tubing revolutions, and when the permitted use time is exceeded the tubing must be shifted or replaced.

questions.question: According to section 4.1.1, why is the isolator the strongest SA option for prolonged continuous or campaign production?

options.A: After the initial biodecontamination the environmental quality is very high and it can run for a long time without opening
options.B: No environmental monitoring is needed inside an isolator
options.C: An isolator in a Grade D background can be opened at any time
options.D: The mechanisms inside an isolator generate no particles

questions.explanation: After the initial surface biodecontamination the environmental quality inside an isolator is very high, and it is designed to run for a long time without being opened, so it is the strongest SA option for prolonged processes. An isolator still needs EM; opening the door would destroy this advantage; and the mechanisms still generate particles.

questions.question: According to section 4.3, which category of factors affects whether the fill speed is acceptable but has no significant effect on the choice of filling technology?

options.A: Cycle-time limits, such as pump cycles and conveyor pacing
options.B: Priming time, batch size, shift length and batch changeover time
options.C: Acceleration/deceleration limits, such as foaming, viscosity or dripping characteristics
options.D: Dose accuracy requirements for the fill curve (such as container type, single or multiple dose)

questions.explanation: Section 4.3 divides the factors limiting speed into three categories: cycle-time limits, acceleration/deceleration limits, and other factors that affect the overall fill duration (priming, batch size, shift length, changeover time). The first two categories affect technology selection; the last affects only whether the speed is acceptable and has no significant effect on technology selection.

questions.question: According to section 4.4, how should the transfer of foam-prone products into a vessel be designed?

options.A: Spray from a high point at the top of the vessel, to speed up mixing
options.B: Set the agitation speed at the highest validated condition, to mix uniformly and quickly
options.C: Feed from the bottom through a J-tube, with subsequent additions made below the liquid surface
options.D: Place the vessel lower than the filling pump, to reduce head pressure and reduce splashing and dripping

questions.explanation: Foam-prone products should not be allowed to fall over a long distance; a dip tube (J-tube) should be used to move the inlet to the lowest point, or the vessel should be fed from the bottom, and every later addition should be made below the liquid surface. The agitation speed should be set slightly above the minimum validated condition to avoid drawing in air, and placing the vessel higher than the filling pump is what helps avoid entrained air.

questions.question: According to section 4.5, why may a TP system not be the most suitable choice for products that tend to drip?

options.A: A TP cannot actively suck back using a reverse stroke
options.B: The orifice of a TP increases the product's surface tension
options.C: A TP must be paired with a closing needle to operate, which adds assembly complexity
options.D: The pinch valve of a TP cannot close quickly

questions.explanation: Liquid retraction uses a small stroke in the direction opposite to filling to draw the product slightly back into the needle and form a meniscus, so that surface tension holds the last drop. A TP cannot perform an active reverse stroke and can only approximate the effect by closing the pinch valve quickly, so it is not necessarily suitable for drip-prone products. RPP, DP and PP can all use a servo for the reverse motion. A closing needle is an optional countermeasure, not a requirement for operation.

questions.question: According to section 4.6, in what situation is recirculation more suitable than simple agitation?

options.A: The product is a true solution and does not settle at all, even during short stops or shift-change shutdowns
options.B: The product is very sensitive to shear
options.C: The vessel is very small and located right next to the filling machine
options.D: The connecting lines between the vessel and the filling system are long, and settling in the lines needs to be controlled

questions.explanation: Agitation alone only keeps the product moving inside the vessel; when the connecting lines are long, settling occurs in the lines. Recirculation keeps the bulk vessel, the intermediate vessel and the whole flow path moving. For a true solution, agitation without recirculation is enough, and shear sensitivity, if anything, may limit how or for how long recirculation can be used.

questions.question: According to section 4.7, why must relative humidity be tightly controlled when filling refrigerated products, yet not set too low?

options.A: High humidity makes stoppers absorb water and swell; too low a humidity makes the product surface freeze
options.B: High humidity interferes with the VPHP cycle; too low a humidity makes the HEPA filter media brittle and cracked
options.C: To prevent condensation on needles and elsewhere diluting the product; too low a humidity generates static that interferes with weighing
options.D: High humidity lowers product viscosity; too low a humidity increases foaming during filling

questions.explanation: Cold vessels and tubing, and especially the outside of the filling needles, may have condensation, and the water droplets can dilute the product and compromise sterility, so humidity must be tightly controlled; but a %RH that is too low makes components pick up static, which affects weighing, causes dripping or makes component handling difficult. The document does not mention the cause-and-effect relationships in the other options.

questions.question: According to section 4.10, which of the following is consistent with the design principles for robots in an aseptic filling area?

options.A: The arm may move directly above open containers to shorten the path
options.B: Servos and cams are placed outside the barrier or below working height, and sealed
options.C: The arm should stay close to the return air openings of an open RABS so that generated particles are removed
options.D: Use the fastest movement when approaching open containers, to minimize the time the container opening is exposed

questions.explanation: The design principles include placing servos and cams outside the aseptic barrier or below working height and sealing them; the arm must not be above open containers or components, nor near locations with a backflow risk such as the return air openings of an oRABS; and the slowest movement should be used when approaching open containers, to reduce turbulence. The effect on unidirectional flow should also be confirmed with CFD and smoke studies.

questions.question: According to the example in section 5.1.2, for an RTU line with 10 filling stations, an IPC rate of 1% and 100 containers per nest, how many nests need to be held in the quarantine buffer pending subsequent weighing results?
questions.explanation: Only 1 nest in every 10 is weighed, one row of 10 containers (10 stations x 1 row), so the 10 nests between two weighings must wait in the quarantine buffer for the next weighing result. The document also requires a quarantine buffer for all intermittent in-line weighing, and nested lines must be able to track, isolate or discard whole nests.

questions.question: According to section 5.1.3, if a 100% weighing system performs re-dosing (top-up), what is required with respect to the APS?

options.A: It should be executed or simulated in the APS, because the longer filling time increases risk
options.B: Re-dosing is an automation function, so it does not need to be included in the APS design
options.C: Only its dosing accuracy needs to be tested in OQ, and it need not be put into the APS design
options.D: It needs to be included only for very small fill volumes

questions.explanation: Re-dosing extends the filling time of a single container and may increase risk, so when it is actually used it should be executed or simulated as a standard part of the APS. The document also mentions that very small fill volumes are generally not suitable for re-dosing, so the option "It needs to be included only for very small fill volumes" is the opposite of the truth.

questions.question: According to section 5.2, how is the fill target usually set when statistical dose control is used?

options.A: The target is set directly at the lower limit, to reduce overfill
options.B: The target is set further from the lower limit, so the operating window shrinks or overfill increases
options.C: The target is exactly the same as for a 100% IPC line, with no adjustment
options.D: Because only samples are checked, no reject limit needs to be set

questions.explanation: With statistical sampling the weight of each container is not known, so a safety margin must be left for containers that are not weighed; the target is therefore set further from the lower limit, and the reject limit is also set further from the maximum and minimum limits. The result is a smaller operating window for products with both upper and lower limits, and more overfill for products with only a lower limit. When a sample fails, all product between the last passing check and this one must be rejected.

questions.topic: Manual dose adjustment on stable pumps
questions.question: According to section 5.2.2.2, why do many systems require "manual" dose adjustment for stable pumps such as an RPP or rolling DP?

options.A: Regulations prohibit filling machines from adjusting the dose automatically
options.B: These pumps have no servo drive, so automatic dose adjustment is mechanically impossible
options.C: Manual adjustment responds faster than automatic adjustment
options.D: To avoid overcorrection from automatically correcting for random variation

questions.explanation: The dose of an RPP and DP does not drift between the start and end of a batch, so if it were automatically corrected for ordinary random variation it would be overcorrected and the weight would oscillate; many stable filling machines therefore require manual adjustment. For a PP, the dose decreases because of tubing stress, so automatic correction is mostly used; for a TP, because the pressure keeps changing with liquid level, automatic correction is standard practice.

questions.question: According to section 5.3.2, for a stable process with Cpk = 1.33, about how many containers per million are expected at most to fall outside the dose limits?

options.A: About 2,699
options.B: About 6
options.C: About 66

questions.explanation: According to Table 5.3.2-1, a Cpk of 1.33 corresponds to about 4 sigma, with at most about 66 per million outside the limits; a Cpk of 1.00 (3 sigma) gives about 2,699 ppm, 1.50 about 6 ppm, and 1.67 (5 sigma) about 0. Industry generally accepts a Cpk between 1 and 1.33.

questions.question: According to section 6.0, when a new container or closure is being considered, what is one of the most important practices?

options.A: Involve potential component suppliers in equipment design and selection as early as possible
options.B: Select the container only after equipment FAT is complete
options.C: Complete PPQ first, then confirm compatibility with the supplier
options.D: Always reuse the format parts of the existing vials

questions.explanation: The material and design of the container closure affect the filling line and the closing system, so when a new container or closure is adopted the component supplier must be involved as early as possible in equipment design and selection, to ensure suitability and compatibility. Confirming only after FAT or PPQ is too costly, and reusing old format parts cannot accommodate a new design.

questions.question: According to section 6.1, how does needle-through-septum filling of a presterilized, fully closed vial improve SA?

options.A: A crimp seal is added after filling, to strengthen the septum seal
options.B: No CCI test is needed once filling is complete
options.C: The need for a barrier system such as an isolator or RABS is eliminated entirely
options.D: The container stays closed during filling, and the septum is then thermally sealed to maintain integrity

questions.explanation: Filling with a fine needle through the septum keeps the sterile container closed during filling, and the septum is then sealed by thermal fusion to maintain its integrity, which improves SA. The document does not say that CCI testing or a barrier can be dispensed with, and adding a crimp seal is not the point of this design.

questions.question: According to section 6.1, what needs special consideration in the APS design for multi-chamber containers?

options.A: Only the last chamber to be filled needs to be challenged
options.B: A single-chamber container can be substituted, to simplify the design
options.C: Ensure that every part is appropriately wetted and challenged
options.D: Multi-chamber containers do not need to be included in the APS

questions.explanation: One of the evaluation factors listed in section 6.1 is APS complexity: the appropriate surfaces must be wetted and every part of a multi-stage fill must be evaluated, so every part of a multi-chamber container must be appropriately challenged in the APS. Testing only one chamber or using a substitute container cannot cover them.

questions.question: According to section 6.1, what might the "transport risks" of a new container closure system include?

options.A: Lower cabin pressure or residual bubbles causing stopper displacement
options.B: Printed fonts on the outer carton label fading and blurring during transport
options.C: Inaccurate temperature loggers on transport vehicles
options.D: Secondary packaging cartons deforming from moisture

questions.explanation: The transport risks described in the document are atypical risks caused by the special design or functional specification of the container closure system itself, for example reduced cabin pressure causing the stopper to move, or residual bubbles letting the stopper shift during air transport. Labels, temperature loggers and cartons are not risks of the container closure design itself.

questions.question: According to section 6.1, what complexity may IPC bring for multi-chamber containers?

options.A: A single weighing of the final product is enough
options.B: Checkpoints and rejection strategies may be needed after each fill and each closure placement
options.C: IPC can be replaced entirely by downstream visual inspection
options.D: IPC is needed only for the first chamber

questions.explanation: To ensure that every chamber is filled to the correct volume and properly sealed, IPC checkpoints may be needed after every fill and every closure placement, so different segregation and rejection strategies are needed at several points. Weighing once, checking only the first chamber or replacing it with visual inspection cannot confirm each chamber.

questions.question: According to section 7.3.1, where is raised stopper detection usually located, and why is a vision system considered state of the art?

options.A: Before the filling needles, because a vision system can check fill height, needle position and container at the same time
options.B: Before the capping station (when the capping station is not in Grade A), because it can catch more position variations
options.C: After the visual inspection station, because its build cost is lowest
options.D: At the lyophilizer outlet, because it can measure residual oxygen at the same time

questions.explanation: When the capping station is not within a Grade A environment (for example, only a Grade A air supply), the detector is usually placed before capping to check all containers for missing or displaced stoppers, and failures are forcibly rejected. A vision system can detect and reject more kinds of position variation, whereas a sensor is less sensitive to changes in the three-dimensional position of the stopper.

questions.question: According to section 7.3.2, which insertion method is more commonly used for coated or silicone-free syringe stoppers?

options.A: Vented insertion, because it is referenced to the finger flange and gives the most consistent positioning
options.B: Long-tube vacuum-assisted vented insertion
options.C: Vacuum insertion (vacuum bell), which has the least precompression
options.D: Unvented mechanical insertion, because it has the lowest cost

questions.explanation: Vented insertion compresses the stopper first, which may damage the coating or wrinkle the ribs of a silicone-free stopper, causing cosmetic defects and a leakage risk. Vacuum insertion has very little precompression and best protects coated stoppers; the short-tube vacuum-assisted version adds almost no extra compression either. The long-tube version compresses too much and is not suitable for coated stoppers.

questions.question: According to section 7.4.1, which statement about the conditions for applying vial crimp seals is correct?

options.A: At least under a continuous Grade A air supply; the seal need not be sterile
options.B: It must be performed in a Grade C environment, and aluminum seals must always be sterilized first
options.C: It can be done in a Grade D environment, because the vial is already fully stoppered
options.D: It must be in the same zone as the filling station and must not be separated by a barrier

questions.explanation: The mechanical seal must be applied at least under a Grade A air supply continuous with the filling line, to protect vials that are fully stoppered but not yet capped; the seal itself need not be sterile. Crimping aluminum caps generates many particles, so the capping equipment is often separated from the stoppering section by a physical barrier (usually with a mousehole); the option "It must be in the same zone as the filling station and must not be separated by a barrier" states the opposite.

questions.question: According to section 7.5, why must a cartridge disc seal be fully sterilized and applied inside the aseptic boundary close to the filling point?

options.A: Because the aluminum cap must first be heated and softened in the aseptic area before it can be crimped into shape
options.B: Because regulations require all aluminum caps and stoppers to be sterilized first
options.C: Because it is used only for lyophilized products
options.D: The elastomer and aluminum seal are applied in one step; being close to the filling point shortens the exposure of the open container

questions.explanation: The elastomer and the aluminum seal of a disc seal are applied in one step, which directly closes the open container, so it must be fully sterilized, the equipment must be inside the aseptic boundary, and it must be close to the filling point to shorten the exposure time of the open container. Crimping generates particles, so airflow must not blow from the crimping station toward the filling station, and the crimping technology should minimize particles.

questions.question: According to section 7.7, what is recommended so that CCI validation samples cover lot-to-lot variability of the components?

options.A: Use only one lot of vials and stoppers, to reduce variables
options.B: Use multiple (for example three) sets of unique component lot pairings
options.C: Test only the combination of the largest and smallest component dimensions
options.D: Replace actual testing with the supplier's CoA

questions.explanation: To cover lot-to-lot variability, validation samples should consider multiple (for example three) unique pairings of component lots, such as stopper lot A with vial lot A, stopper lot B with vial lot A, and so on. In addition, when the capping force is variable, CCI testing should be performed at high, medium and low settings.

questions.topic: Establishing Grade A: isolator vs RABS
questions.question: According to section 8.1, how does the timing of establishing Grade A conditions differ between an isolator and a RABS?

options.A: Both establish Grade A before the sterilized parts are installed
options.B: A RABS has its sterilized parts installed first and the 6-log biodecontamination is done afterwards, the opposite of an isolator
options.C: An isolator has the 6-log biodecontamination done after the sterilized parts are installed; a RABS before installation
options.D: An isolator needs no 6-log procedure and only needs cleaning

questions.explanation: An isolator is cleaned and disinfected, the sterilized parts are installed and the door is closed, and then Grade A is established by an automated 6-log sporicidal biodecontamination (such as VPHP); that is, Grade A is established after the parts are installed. A RABS has Grade A established before the sterilized parts are installed, by cleaning plus 6-log sporicidal high-level disinfection.

questions.question: According to section 8.3, when the filter of a SIP system is in a stainless steel housing outside Grade A and the filter needs to be changed, how should it be handled?

options.A: Stop and split into two lot numbers; perform CIP, SIP of the new filter and pre-use testing, then resume filling
options.B: Do not stop; change the filter in-line, and continue filling after only a visual check and leak check
options.C: After the change, only a post-use integrity test is needed
options.D: After the change, treating the filter housing with VPHP is enough to resume

questions.explanation: With this design, changing the filter exposes the sterile flow path to a lower-grade environment, so filling must stop and the batch be split into two parts with different lot numbers; after the old filter is removed, CIP is performed, the new filter is SIP processed, and filling can resume only after the pre-use integrity test and flush are complete. Changing in-line or surface treatment alone does not address the risk of the opened flow path.

questions.question: According to section 8.6, how are the packaging layers removed when components are manually transferred from Grade B into Grade A?

options.A: All bags are removed inside the Grade B area
options.B: The second-to-last layer is removed at the B-to-A transfer, and the last layer only inside Grade A
options.C: The last layer is removed inside the Grade C area
options.D: All bags are brought into Grade A and removed all at once by the operator under unidirectional flow

questions.explanation: Sterile packaging is removed layer by layer as the components pass through each grade: the second-to-last layer is removed aseptically under unidirectional flow at the Grade B to Grade A transfer, and the final layer only within Grade A. The removed packaging must not touch surfaces inside Grade A. The document also notes that automated transfer is the better practice.

questions.question: According to section 8.8, when may a category 4 mechanical intervention (equipment located in a technical area or gray zone) be opened during the aseptic process?

options.A: The technical area may be opened at any time during the process, as long as quality has approved in advance
options.B: It may be opened during the process, as long as an AVS shows that unidirectional flow is not affected
options.C: Never under any circumstances; the batch must always be terminated
options.D: Only when accessed from a service area segregated from the cleanroom; otherwise filling must be paused

questions.explanation: A technical area that has not been biodecontaminated or disinfected must not be opened during aseptic processing, the only exception being access from a service area segregated from the cleanroom. If access is only possible from inside the cleanroom, filling must be paused, the affected area cleared, then disinfected and the equipment cleaned and sterilized again, which often exceeds hold times and leads to termination. The option "Never under any circumstances; the batch must always be terminated" is wrong because it ignores this exception.

questions.question: According to section 8.9, which of the following EM samplings is event-driven?

options.A: Continuous total particle monitoring throughout the operation
options.B: Settle plates changed at fixed time intervals
options.C: Contact plates/swabs at setup, after interventions, or when personnel leave at the end of work
options.D: Volumetric air sampling at fixed times (hourly)

questions.explanation: The EM sampling plan has both time-driven and event-driven elements: settle plates and volumetric air are sampled at time intervals, whereas contact plates and swabs correspond to specific events such as setup, aseptic interventions, personnel leaving at the end of work, end of batch or campaign changeover. Total particles must be monitored continuously throughout.

questions.question: According to Table 9.1.1.7-1, what is the main residue risk of an RTU container transfer method that uses E-beam for external decontamination?

options.A: Oxidizing residue (hydrogen peroxide)
options.B: There is no residue risk at all
options.C: Ethylene oxide (EtO) residue
options.D: Free radical or ozone residue

questions.explanation: In the residue risk row of the table, on-site processing and RTU plus NTT have none; RTU plus external hydrogen peroxide decontamination has an oxidizing residue risk; and RTU plus E-beam has a free radical or ozone residue risk. EtO is not one of the transfer methods compared in this table.

questions.question: According to section 9.1.1.8, what special risk does a cartridge disc seal have compared with other elastomeric closures?

options.A: It cannot withstand the repeated punctures of multi-dose use
options.B: The integrated crimp seal is applied near the filling machine, which gives a higher risk of particle release
options.C: The material must allow EtO to penetrate, so that the syringe barrel can be sterilized
options.D: It can only be used for products stored at ultra-low temperature

questions.explanation: A disc seal consists of an elastomer disc and a crimp seal, and because the integrated crimping is applied near the filling machine, the risk of particle release is higher than for other elastomers. A multi-dose disc seal in fact has to be self-sealing; the element that must allow EtO penetration is the elastomer of a syringe needle; and the one that tolerates ultra-low temperatures is a snap closure.

questions.question: According to section 9.1.2, which of the following is NOT among the goals that closure pretreatment and subsequent packaging design must achieve?

options.A: Keep an appropriate amount of moisture on the stopper surface to ease insertion
options.B: Reduce closures sticking or tangling together
options.C: Prevent separation of assembled closures (such as disc seals)
options.D: Prevent deformation, such as bending of aluminum parts or plungers

questions.explanation: Section 9.1.2 requires pretreatment and packaging design to reduce closures sticking or tangling, prevent deformation, prevent separation or misalignment of assembled closures, prevent one-piece caps from breaking at their connection points, and ensure dryness (especially important for moisture-sensitive products and lyophilization stoppers). Retaining moisture goes directly against "ensure dryness".

questions.question: According to section 9.1.4, which statement about crimp seals and caps is correct?

options.A: All RABS must use sterile crimp seals, regardless of capper location
options.B: Aluminum caps never need to be sterilized under any circumstances
options.C: It is recommended to transfer them in bulk in soft-bag RTP to reduce impact
options.D: When the capping station is within Grade A of an isolator, the aluminum caps must be sterile

questions.explanation: When the capper is within the Grade A environment of an isolator, the crimp seals and caps must be sterilized; for most conventional operations (such as RABS) it is not mandatory and can be decided according to the CCS. When handled in bulk, damage and deformation of the caps must be prevented, so soft-bag RTP is generally not recommended.

questions.question: According to section 9.1.3, what should be watched for when bulk-supplied stoppers are fed by vibration?

options.A: The stronger the vibration the better, to avoid jams
options.B: The vibration area needs no separate airflow study
options.C: Control particles at that location, and demonstrate by airflow studies that unidirectional flow is controlled during vibration
options.D: As long as RTU stoppers are used, vibratory feeding generates no particles at all

questions.explanation: Vibration and friction between components generate or release particles, so particles at these locations must be measured and controlled, and the feeding mechanism must not damage the components. Airflow studies in Grade A must show that unidirectional flow remains controlled during vibration, and the same applies where containers collide, such as turntables and accumulation tables. RTU components do not mean that vibration generates no particles.

questions.question: According to section 10.2, what does the "ring of concern" at the docking point of an RTP alpha/beta port refer to?

options.A: The interface at the docking surfaces, which can still be exposed during unloading if not properly disinfected
options.B: The dead spot inside the RTP container that steam or sterilant reaches least easily
options.C: The seam between the glove port and the barrier wall, where residues accumulate most easily
options.D: The breathable area of the material of the beta bag

questions.explanation: The alpha and beta ports are designed so that non-sterile outer surfaces do not touch the components or the filling area, but if the docking surfaces are not carefully treated and regularly disinfected, decontaminated or sterilized, the "ring of concern" at the interface can still allow slight exposure during unloading. Section 10.4 also requires that this ring be carefully disinfected or decontaminated.

questions.question: According to section 10.2, why should the selection of RTP transfer containers be coordinated with the component supplier?

options.A: Because the transfer container must be sterilized in the same lot as the product
options.B: Because the beta port can be used only once
options.C: Because the alpha port is a consumable that must be replaced with a new one every batch
options.D: Port designs are mostly proprietary and may not be compatible with existing equipment

questions.explanation: The alpha/beta port connection designs of transfer container suppliers are often proprietary and may not be compatible with the alpha ports already permanently installed on the equipment, so coordination with the component supplier is needed to ensure the container fits the equipment's alpha port. The document does not mention the other options.

questions.question: According to section 10.2, when a transfer container holding product-contact materials (such as tubing and stoppers) is treated with a rapid hydrogen peroxide cycle, what must be confirmed before opening?

options.A: The outer surface of the container is completely dry
options.B: Residual H2O2 inside has fallen to a suitable level, with particular care for polymers
options.C: A 6-log spore challenge has been completed and biological indicator results obtained
options.D: The inside of the container has cooled to room temperature

questions.explanation: Residual hydrogen peroxide can oxidize and degrade the product, so when a connected transfer container is treated with a rapid cycle, the residual H2O2 inside must be reduced to a suitable level before opening and exposing the product; particular care is needed when the container holds polymers that absorb hydrogen peroxide. The other options are not conditions the document sets for opening.

questions.question: According to section 10.3, why is guided conveyance (feed screw, star wheel, etc.) better than simple back-pressure pushing for containers with small openings or narrow necks?

options.A: Guided conveyance always has a higher line speed
options.B: Back-pressure pushing makes the containers too hot
options.C: It aligns precisely with the filling needle, avoiding needle strikes, chipped openings or spray onto the neck
options.D: Back-pressure pushing cannot be used for RTU containers and is only for bulk vials

questions.explanation: Guided conveyance positions the container precisely under the filling needle. A small opening must be centered accurately, otherwise the needle will strike the opening (chipping the sealing surface or bending the needle) or spray product onto the neck, which affects closure. An overload sensor only prevents needle strike damage and cannot solve every alignment problem. Back-pressure and accumulation zones also increase the risk of scratching.

questions.question: According to section 10.4, among the transfer methods for dry-heat treated materials, why have metal trays fallen out of favor?

options.A: They seal poorly, unless a secondary treatment such as hydrogen peroxide is applied after transfer in
options.B: Metal trays cannot withstand the high temperatures needed for dry-heat sterilization and depyrogenation
options.C: Metal trays release ozone after dry heat
options.D: Regulations prohibit any metal items in the critical zone of Grade A

questions.explanation: Many polymers cannot tolerate dry-heat temperatures, so dry-heat materials cannot be wrapped in sterile packaging, and there are only three transfer options: a transfer container with a dry-heat-resistant alpha-beta port, metal trays, or an oven connected directly to the filling area. Metal trays have fallen out of favor because of poor sealing, unless a secondary treatment such as hydrogen peroxide can be applied after transfer in.

questions.question: According to section 11.5, what is the main benefit of two sterilizing filters in series?

options.A: The overall filtration flow rate can be doubled
options.B: If the downstream test fails, the upstream filter can be tested; if it passes, the batch disposition is unaffected
options.C: With two in series, both the pre-use and post-use integrity tests can be omitted
options.D: The filters can be used for more than one working day

questions.explanation: With two sterilizing filters in series, if the integrity test of the downstream filter fails, the upstream filter can still be tested; if the upstream filter passes, the batch disposition is not affected. Series filters do not double the flow rate, cannot replace integrity testing and do not extend the use time limit. Another common design is two parallel flow paths, switching when the pressure differential rises.

questions.question: According to section 11.6, what are the two main failure modes if filling (and thus filtration) time is prolonged?

options.A: Shedding of filter membrane fibers and pressure corrosion of the housing
options.B: Product crystallization and temperature rise
options.C: Proliferation of bulk bioburden and microbial penetration of the filter membrane
options.D: Progressive aging of the filling tubing, and dose drift of the filling pump

questions.explanation: When the time is prolonged, first, bulk held before filtration in a non-sterile intermediate vessel may see bioburden grow and increase the load on the filter; second, upstream microorganisms may multiply and grow through the membrane. A sterile transfer vessel can therefore be considered to speed up filtration; that vessel must be kept under positive pressure, fitted with a sterilizing vent filter, and its sterile hold time must be validated.

questions.question: According to section 11.4, which type of filter is considered the first choice for SUS, and why?

options.A: Cartridge filter, because it can be SIP processed in a housing
options.B: Ceramic cartridge, because it can be reused for many years
options.C: Prefilter, because it can reduce bioburden
options.D: Capsule filter, because its housing is molded in one piece and it integrates well with the flow path

questions.explanation: A capsule filter comes with a pressure-resistant molded polymer housing and connections, and integrates well with the flow path, so it is regarded as the first choice for SUS. A cartridge filter must be installed in an equipment housing, can be autoclaved offline or SIP processed on hard piping, and is better suited to fixed piping systems. The other two options are not filter types compared in section 11.4.

questions.question: According to section 11.10, what risk is specific to an RPP in the design of the filtration flow path?

options.A: If the buffer volume between pump and filter is insufficient, back-flow through the filter may occur
options.B: The pulsating pressure generated by an RPP directly tears or damages the filter membrane
options.C: The pressure drop of the filter throws off the dose control of a downstream TP system
options.D: There is no additional risk

questions.explanation: Table 11.10-1 and the text state that if the volume between the pump and the filter (manifold or reservoir) is insufficient, an RPP carries the risk of back-flow through the filter; pulsation damaging the membrane is a DP risk; the pressure drop without a sterile receiving vessel is a TP risk; and a PP is listed as having no additional risk.

questions.question: According to section 11.11, what is the core concept of the control strategy for products that can be neither sterile filtered nor terminally sterilized (for example some suspensions or cell therapy products)?

options.A: As long as the finished product sterility test passes, that is enough
options.B: "The process is the product": every sterile input must be assured individually
options.C: Use a larger pore size filter, so that the cells can pass through and sterility is maintained
options.D: Replace the sterilization validation of each component with an APS

questions.explanation: Sterility assurance for such products comes from the combination of all sterile inputs, so every component must be individually assured sterile (including filtering those components that can be filtered first), and the combining process must provide the highest SA; shortening the flow path and ensuring its integrity after sterilization is key. Neither a sterility test nor an APS can replace this item-by-item assurance, and a larger pore size would lose the sterilizing function.

questions.question: According to section 12.5, how are high-value products often wound down after the bulk low/low-low level alarm is triggered, to reduce loss?

options.A: Stop everything immediately and scrap all filled containers, including those that are full
options.B: Increase the filling speed to fill all remaining product quickly before the level runs out
options.C: Shut down individual filling paths in stages, finally stop completely, and discard those not fully filled
options.D: Switch to manual pouring from the intermediate vessel directly into containers

questions.explanation: After the alarm triggers, the filling machine starts a shutdown, clearance or emptying mode; for high-value products the shutdown can be staged, first closing some filling paths and finally stopping all, and discarding all containers that are not completely filled. The top-up filling technique used in the priming phase can also be used to make sure the last containers are filled correctly, and these end-of-batch procedures must be included in process validation.

questions.question: According to section 12.6, if a nested syringe has an out-of-control dose at one filling needle and the choice is to discard only the individual syringes, what is required?

options.A: A verification mechanism, such as robotic tracking or independent four-eyes review
options.B: It is enough to note the affected needle position, tub and nest numbers in the batch record
options.C: The operator on duty visually judges and removes them
options.D: No additional verification is needed, because the system handles it automatically

questions.explanation: Discarding individual syringes is more complex and needs a verification mechanism: a robot (tracking of reject marks or physical segregation), or independent review under the four-eyes principle, to ensure that all affected syringes are discarded. Discarding the whole tub is more conservative and simpler for the quality system and documentation.

questions.question: According to section 13.1, until when must EM (total particles and viable) continue at the end of a batch?

options.A: Until filling of the last container is complete
options.B: Until stoppering of the last container is complete
options.C: Until all operators have completed exit monitoring and left the cleanroom
options.D: Until all filled containers are fully closed, sealed and have left the filling line

questions.explanation: EM must continue until all filled containers are fully closed, sealed and have left the filling line. In a campaign where the environment continues to be used, it must also continue through the changeover and setup of the next batch. EM of critical surfaces (such as filling needles and feed bowls) must be sampled before major disassembly, and the sequence must be written into the SOP in advance.

questions.question: According to section 13.5, at what point is wash-in-place (WIP) usually scheduled after processing a highly potent or hazardous product?

options.A: Before the bulk product is used up, so that residual liquid does not dry on the line and become harder to remove
options.B: After the product is used up and final EM and removal of unused components are complete, and before the barrier is opened
options.C: After the barrier is opened, with personnel entering to spray-wash manually
options.D: Before final EM sampling, so that the wash liquid does not affect the samples

questions.explanation: The purpose of WIP is to let the barrier be opened safely without exposing personnel or the external environment, so it must be run before the containment barrier is opened, and after the bulk is used up and drained, final EM is complete and the samples are sealed, and unused containers and closures are removed. The WIP scope runs from below the HEPA to the return air openings, and the HEPA must not be wetted.

questions.question: According to section 13.6, how is the formal line clearance check at the end of a batch usually done?

options.A: The operator who performed the clearance signs it off alone
options.B: The operator of the next batch checks at the start of that batch
options.C: After the operator's preliminary clearance, QA independent of the clearance work reviews it
options.D: The equipment's automated clearance mode replaces the manual check

questions.explanation: Clearance can be done more than once: the operator first performs a preliminary clearance and confirms that all batch materials are documented, then a formal clearance check is made, reviewed by QA (or a designee) independent of the clearance work, after which the line can be released. The aim is to prevent mix-ups between batches and to ensure that samples and rejects have been accounted for.

questions.question: According to Table 14.2-1, which statement about the background environment required for each type of barrier system is correct?

options.A: All barrier systems need at least a Grade B background
options.B: An isolator needs a Grade B background, while a RABS can be in Grade C
options.C: Both open and closed isolators need at least a Grade B background
options.D: Open isolator at least C, closed isolator at least D; RABS is B

questions.explanation: Table 14.2-1: the background of an open isolator is at least Grade C and of a closed isolator at least Grade D; both cRABS and oRABS must be in a Grade B background, because the interior of the barrier may be exposed to the outside environment during processing (an oRABS is itself an incomplete enclosure).

questions.question: According to section 14.1, by definition what is opening a RABS door after disinfection is complete (including for setup)?

options.A: A routine operation that needs no special control
options.B: An intervention, which needs protection by overhead unidirectional flow and should be minimized
options.C: A deviation, and the batch must be terminated immediately
options.D: Closed operation, not an intervention, as long as the operator wears sterile gloves and works under overhead unidirectional flow

questions.explanation: A RABS is fully disinfected before setup, and any door opening afterwards (including setup) counts as an intervention; entry after disinfection must have overhead unidirectional flow protection covering the door area, door-opening interventions should be minimized by design, and they are managed by detailed procedures. An isolator, by contrast, is opened only at the start of setup and at the end of the batch or campaign, and used again after the door is closed and biodecontamination is done.

questions.question: According to section 14.2, what is the main difference in airflow design between a cRABS and an oRABS?

options.A: A cRABS is positive pressure, with built-in fans and base return; an oRABS returns to room low walls
options.B: An oRABS is a positive-pressure sealed system, while a cRABS shares low-wall return openings with the cleanroom
options.C: The airflow design of both is identical, and they differ only in the number and position of doors
options.D: A cRABS uses no HEPA fans and relies entirely on supply air from the room's air conditioning

questions.explanation: In an oRABS the HEPA unidirectional flow passes down through the process and returns to the cleanroom's low-wall return openings to be recirculated, and the enclosure does not seal tightly to the equipment or room; a cRABS is a positive-pressure system with an integrated HEPA fan unit and the return openings integrated in the equipment base. A cRABS is often used for highly potent products.

questions.question: According to section 14.0, how do most regulators view a conventional aseptic cleanroom without controlled separation of personnel from the filling operation?

options.A: It is a design that meets current standards, as long as EM and APS results remain consistently good
options.B: It is suitable only for the production of clinical batches
options.C: It is a legacy system needing improvement; before upgrading, a risk assessment should be done and regulators engaged
options.D: It has been banned outright and production must stop immediately

questions.explanation: Aseptic processing should separate personnel from the process, usually by means of a barrier. Most regulators regard a standard aseptic cleanroom without controlled separation as a legacy system needing improvement; before a barrier upgrade is completed, continued operation should be supported by a risk assessment and risk reduction, and communicated to regulators. The document does not say it has been banned outright.

questions.question: According to Table 14.2-1, what is the requirement for the chamber leak test (the leak test before biodecontamination) for the three types of barrier?

options.A: It must be performed on all three types of barrier
options.B: Only the oRABS needs it, because its pressure differential with the room cannot be actively controlled
options.C: None of the three types needs it
options.D: Isolator yes; cRABS depending on design; oRABS not applicable

questions.explanation: In the maintenance and periodic testing items of Table 14.2-1, chamber integrity/gas tightness is "yes" for an isolator, "possibly (depending on design)" for a cRABS and "no" for an oRABS. By contrast, maintenance and integrity testing of the glove ports is needed for all three.

questions.question: According to section 15.0, which category of utility is considered the most critical?

options.A: Those in direct contact with the product or with equipment that contacts it, such as CIP, SIP and nitrogen
options.B: Lighting and general electrical power, because a power loss immediately interrupts the whole filling line and HVAC
options.C: Heat exchange fluids such as cooling water, because it is used in the largest quantity, has the longest piping and is the hardest to control
options.D: Hydraulic systems, because leaks are the hardest to detect

questions.explanation: Among the utilities listed, those in direct contact with the product, and those that contact equipment in direct contact with the product (such as CIP, SIP and nitrogen), are the most critical, and piping design and installation can refer to ASME BPE and Annex 1. The general principle is that utilities should not be in the cleanroom unless unavoidable.

questions.question: According to section 15.1, when aqueous utilities such as CIP/SIP remain inside the cleanroom, what should be watched for regarding piping connections?

options.A: Connections should be replaced with hoses as far as possible, to absorb vibration
options.B: Connections need to be checked only at annual maintenance
options.C: Thermal expansion and contraction can loosen connections, so routine checks are needed, and welding is preferred in sensitive areas
options.D: As long as they are disinfected regularly, how tight the connections are does not affect risk

questions.explanation: Water always carries a risk of microbial growth. CIP/SIP avoids aseptic assembly, but keeping the related utilities in the cleanroom is still a significant risk, so points of use should be checked frequently for leaks; thermal expansion and contraction during circulation or sanitization can loosen connections, so checks of sanitary connection tightness should be part of routine status checks, with welding preferred in sensitive areas.

questions.question: According to section 16.2, which factors determine the fill dose of a VPPF?

options.A: The outer diameter of the auger, and the number of rotations into the same container
options.B: The dosing chamber volume, the vacuum level, and the number of doses into the same container
options.C: The vibration frequency of the vibratory feeder bowl, and the duration in seconds of each discharge
options.D: Powder temperature and the relative humidity of the filling chamber

questions.explanation: A VPPF draws powder into a dosing chamber by vacuum and compacts it into a slug, which is then blown into the container with dry sterile air; the dose is determined by the dosing chamber volume (depth and diameter), the vacuum level (which compacts the powder) and the number of doses into the same container. The auger outer diameter and number of rotations are the dose determinants of an AF.

questions.question: According to section 16.2.1, what supporting measures are needed when a VPPF uses a super plate (integrated base plate) design?

options.A: The whole assembly is assembled manually in Grade A, so no separate sterilization is needed
options.B: Once adopted, the AVS and APS can be omitted
options.C: Assembly only in Grade D is enough before it goes directly on the machine
options.D: A dedicated cart carries it into the autoclave, and continuous Grade A is maintained from the unloading end to the line

questions.explanation: The super plate lets the dosing wheel, hopper connection and utility connections be assembled in advance on one base plate in Grade C, the whole assembly is sterilized and moved to the aseptic area, and only one or two aseptic connections are needed to install it. The supporting measure is a dedicated cart that goes into the autoclave, with a continuous Grade A unidirectional flow zone maintained from the autoclave unloading end during transport to the line.

questions.question: According to section 16.2.5, why may the position of total particle monitoring probes differ in powder filling compared with liquid filling?

options.A: Powder may cause false positives, so probes may need to be placed higher, with the reason documented
options.B: Powder filling needs no total particle monitoring
options.C: The probe must be placed directly below the dosing disc
options.D: The probe is used only during the setup phase

questions.explanation: Regulators expect viable and total particle monitoring throughout aseptic filling, but powder itself may interfere with monitoring, so probe positions must be evaluated to reduce product-caused false positives, and may need to be higher than the usual working height in liquid filling, with an explanation and documentation. If the powder inhibits the culture media, special EM materials must be used.

questions.question: According to section 16.2.8, how is a plugged dosing chamber in a VPPF during operation generally recommended to be handled?

options.A: Stop immediately and change the whole dosing disc on the spot
options.B: Reject the containers associated with that chamber (on 100% weighing equipment), and changing the disc midway is not recommended
options.C: The operator clears the screen on the spot through the glove port with a sterile tool, recalibrates the weight and continues filling
options.D: Ignore it for now and deal with it all after the batch ends

questions.explanation: The typical approach is to reject the containers associated with that chamber (on 100% weighing equipment). Changing the dosing disc during a run is a major intervention requiring another sterilized disc, line clearance, performing the intervention and taking EM samples, then recalibrating the weight, so it is not recommended. The likelihood of plugging can be lowered by shortening the filling time per batch and optimizing the powder and airflow characteristics.

questions.question: According to section 16.2.11, what is the scope of CIP/SIP that a VPPF can perform?

options.A: All components can be CIP/SIP processed
options.B: Only the dosing disc can be SIP processed
options.C: No CIP/SIP is possible at all
options.D: Only the bulk-feed part

questions.explanation: Only the bulk-feed components of a VPPF can be CIP/SIP processed; other parts must be removed and cleaned by hand or in a parts washer (the screens often in an ultrasonic bath), then sterilized. The dosing disc, drum and needles are cleaned and sterilized offline and then aseptically assembled in a downflow booth. Partial CIP/SIP also adds cost and complexity of utilities and validation.

questions.question: According to sections 16.2.12 and 16.3.11, why is an AF usually preferable to a VPPF when handling highly potent or toxic powders?

options.A: An AF conveys powder mechanically, generates little dust and can be CIP processed; a VPPF needs offline cleaning
options.B: An AF fills significantly faster, so the exposure time is shorter
options.C: An AF is a closed system, so no EM is needed during operation
options.D: A VPPF cannot be installed in an isolator and can only be used on a RABS

questions.explanation: An AF conveys powder mechanically with an auger, generates little dust and can be cleaned in place, which suits highly potent products; a VPPF needs offline cleaning and sterilization and doses by air pressure, so the exposure risk is higher with dusty products, unless it can be rinsed in place before the barrier is opened. A VPPF can be used in both a RABS and an isolator, and an AF still needs EM.
