questions.question: According to sections 16.3.4 and 16.3.10, why is an AF considered to need CIP/SIP?

options.A: Regulations require all powder filling machines to be SIP capable
options.B: The materials of an AF cannot withstand the temperature of an autoclave
options.C: Multiple augers and agitators make aseptic assembly extremely difficult
options.D: An AF doses with compressed air, so the lines must be sterilized

questions.explanation: An AF has multiple augers and agitators and usually cannot be assembled aseptically, and reassembly as an aseptic operation is extremely difficult, so CIP/SIP is needed and the whole procedure must be validated. For this reason, the cost of CIP/SIP is usually not the main differentiator between AF models. An AF does not dose with compressed air.

questions.question: According to section 16.3, which factors mainly determine the fill dose of an AF?

options.A: The dosing chamber volume and the vacuum level
options.B: The auger outer diameter, and the number of rotations into the same container
options.C: The compressed air pressure and blow time
options.D: The hopper height and the total powder weight

questions.explanation: The dose of an AF is determined by the auger outer diameter and the number of rotations into the same container, and adjusting the dose means adjusting the number of rotations. Dosing chamber volume and vacuum level are the VPPF determinants; an AF does not dose with compressed air. The hopper needs appropriate agitation and local exhaust, to avoid back pressure affecting the dose.

questions.question: According to section 17.1, what special requirement does powder filling place on the container compared with liquid filling?

options.A: The container material must be COC, to avoid scratching by powder friction
options.B: Container size need not be considered
options.C: Container selection and neck size are more critical, and the container must be accurately centered
options.D: Containers must always be supplied nested

questions.explanation: In powder filling, container selection and neck size are more critical than in liquid filling, and container centering is a prerequisite for powder entering the container. Neck size affects how much a VPPF can dose at a time, and a small neck also limits the speed of both VPPF and AF; extremely small necks such as ampoules have practical limits for both technologies. The document does not specify material or supply format.

questions.question: According to section 18.0, what is required regarding the position of the receiving hopper when powder bulk is connected through a split valve?

options.A: The receiving hopper must be located in a Grade A environment
options.B: It may be placed in a Grade D gray area, to make changing bags easy
options.C: It must be completely separate from the isolator, to keep dust out
options.D: It need not be considered, because powder does not cause contamination

questions.explanation: A split valve connection requires the receiving hopper to be in a Grade A environment so that the connection stays sterile; if an intrinsic sterile connection device is used instead, the charging point may be in a lower-grade area. Both connector surfaces may carry product residue when disconnected, so containment must be considered for highly potent products, and the microbial and containment requirements decided by risk analysis.

questions.question: According to section 19.2, what risk does powder on the container neck during filling create?

options.A: It affects only appearance, not product quality
options.B: It makes the weight read high and causes false rejects
options.C: Powder left on the neck absorbs moisture and cakes, making it hard to fill the containers of the next batch
options.D: Poor stopper sealing allows oxygen to enter, and this is also hard to see after crimping

questions.explanation: Powder on the neck leaves a poor seal around the stopper, so oxygen may enter during storage; because of the crimp seal, it is also hard to find at first visual inspection. At setup, dose control aimed at the container opening should therefore be strengthened, static control made part of standard environmental control, and necks checked regularly for dust; for nitrogen-filled containers, headspace analysis can demonstrate that the seal is intact.

questions.question: According to section 19.3, what is one of the main reasons a VPPF dose becomes inaccurate?

options.A: The auger wears, so the powder delivered per rotation gradually declines
options.B: Screen blinding
options.C: The hopper temperature is too low, so powder absorbs moisture and cakes, lowering flowability and accuracy
options.D: The compressed air contains oil, making powder stick to the chamber wall

questions.explanation: One of the main reasons for inaccurate VPPF dosing is screen blinding, which affects both powder compaction and discharge; a less common cause is a damaged screen, so screens must be replaced regularly and checked for integrity after cleaning. For an AF, inaccuracy is mainly caused by the powder state changing during the run. Some AF models can adjust dose by dose, whereas a VPPF reacts to the weight trend over several cycles.

questions.question: According to section 19.4, how should a falling hopper powder level at the end of powder filling be managed?

options.A: Continue filling until the hopper is completely empty
options.B: The operator on duty judges from experience when to stop
options.C: During development, define the powder level at which the dose becomes unstable, and stop at that level
options.D: Add the next batch of powder, mix it in and continue filling

questions.explanation: As the powder level falls the dose may become unstable. When filling parameters are developed, the (measurable) powder level at which the dose starts to become unstable should be recorded and defined, filling stopped at that level, and this written into the SOP or batch record. A net-weight filling machine can continue until the rejection rate becomes impractically or non-compliantly high, but it is not simply filled until empty. Mixing in another batch is even less acceptable.

questions.question: According to section 21.1.6, why may the RPP be excluded in Case 1 (monoclonal antibody prefilled syringe)?

options.A: An RPP cannot be installed in an isolator
options.B: 0.5 mL is below the fill range of an RPP
options.C: The product viscosity is too high for an RPP to handle
options.D: The product is sensitive to shear

questions.explanation: After the comparison matrix, PP, TP and DP are the main candidates, because the shear sensitivity of the product may exclude the RPP. An RPP in any case has to be installed within containment; the Case 1 product has low viscosity (water-like); and 0.5 mL is not a reason to exclude an RPP.

questions.question: According to section 21.1.6, if Case 1 needs a smaller fill volume in the future, why might the DP be excluded?

options.A: A DP cannot be used with nested syringes
options.B: About 0.2 mL is already at the lower limit of DP capability
options.C: A DP cannot be made as an SU system
options.D: A DP is not suitable for foam-prone products

questions.explanation: PP, TP and DP all match, and the choice may depend on whether a smaller fill volume will be needed in the future: a DP is already at the lower limit of its capability at about 0.2 mL, so it might be excluded. A DP in fact has SU options (SU favors PP and DP), and CIP/SIP favors TP and DP.

questions.question: According to section 21.1.6, if Case 1 has severe foaming and SU technology is desired, which technology has the advantage, and on what condition?

options.A: PP; provided the number of cycles before the tubing change is within the tubing capability and the batch size
options.B: RPP; provided a ceramic pump is used
options.C: TP; provided a header bag is added
options.D: DP; provided the minimum fill volume is raised above 1 mL in future

questions.explanation: If foaming is severe and SU is wanted, a PP is the strongest candidate, provided that the number of cycles between tubing changes is kept within the capability of the selected tubing and can accommodate the planned batch size. The RPP has already been excluded for shear sensitivity; TP is not an SU preference; and the document sets no such condition for DP.

questions.question: According to section 21.2.6, which two technologies are the leading candidates for Case 2 (250 mL plasma protein LVP bottles)?

options.A: RPP and DP
options.B: TP and DP
options.C: RPP and PP
options.D: PP and TP

questions.explanation: According to the comparison matrix, PP and TP are the leading candidates; the planned fill volume and shear sensitivity may exclude the RPP (two reasons, volume and shear), and the DP is excluded because of volume.

questions.question: According to section 21.2.6, when Case 2 must choose between SU (favoring PP) and CIP/SIP (favoring TP), what factor may drive the decision?

options.A: Whether the product viscosity of 25 mPa-s exceeds the upper limit of a TP
options.B: Whether a diving needle is needed
options.C: The changeover time of each, because batch sizes are small and the flow path must be changed frequently
options.D: Whether sensor filling can be adopted

questions.explanation: PP and TP both match, and the choice may be decided by their changeover times, because batch sizes are small and the flow path has to be changed frequently within a campaign. If foaming is severe and SU is desired, a PP is the strongest candidate provided the SU cost is not excessive for the planned number of batches. A viscosity of 25 mPa-s is not a technical limit.
